name: Cervical traction
lead: Cervical traction is the application of a pulling force to the neck, in a clinic or with a home device, intended to relieve pressure on spinal structures. Physical therapists use it mainly for neck pain with nerve root symptoms such as cervical radiculopathy [1].

In looksmaxxing and posture communities, neck traction devices are discussed as a way to improve neck curvature and forward-head posture. The sources reviewed contain no study of traction for appearance.
Guidelines for cervical traction rest on low-quality evidence, according to a summary of recent literature [1].
infobox: Manual or mechanical neck pulling force

paras: Traction is a set of mechanisms for relieving pressure on the spine or aligning bones, and orthopedic medicine describes skin and skeletal forms. Cervical traction for neck problems is discussed in physical therapy settings, applied manually or with mechanical devices [1]. Some historic traction devices date to antiquity, with an illustrated Greek device from the 2nd century AD in a Byzantine edition of Galen [1].
No studies found on cervical traction for appearance or posture aesthetics.

For pain, Wikipedia summarizes a 2018 meta-analysis reporting that adding traction to physical therapy reduced pain in cervical or lumbar disorders, and a 2020 study reporting that mechanical traction outperformed manual traction; however, the title of that study states that effects in cervical radicular syndrome were statistically significant but not clinically relevant, and a 2017 review found guideline support to be low quality [1]. Researchers have also suggested that inconsistent dosage across studies may explain conflicting results [1]. A 1982 paper on neck traction appears in the physiotherapy literature [2].

The sources reviewed do not detail traction risks. Case reports of unrelated neck conditions in the literature, such as cervical radiculopathy presenting as chest pain, illustrate that neck symptoms can have varied causes [3].

card.summary: Neck pulling devices used in physio for nerve-root pain; no evidence for posture looks.
card.note: Clinical evidence for neck use is low quality; none for appearance.

quick.overview:
Cervical traction gently pulls on the neck, in a clinic or with a home device, to relieve pressure on neck nerves. Posture communities discuss it for neck curve and forward-head posture.

Research is about pain, not looks, and guideline evidence is described as low quality.
quick.mechanism: The proposed idea is that stretching the neck opens space between vertebrae and reduces nerve pressure. Some reviews report short-term pain relief when traction is added to physiotherapy.
quick.risks: The reviewed sources do not detail risks. Neck symptoms can have other causes, so traction is a clinical tool rather than an appearance treatment.
